newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac warns left on privatisation.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac warns left on privatisation.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac warned France's left-wing government on Monday it could slam the door to foreign alliances if it kept control of commercial companies.
The conservative head of state also criticised as "obsolete and absurd" government plans to revive administrative controls on layoffs by private firms, which were scrapped in 1986.

"The state today no longer has any place in the management of competitive industries," Chirac said in a Bastille Day television interview, his first since being forced to share power with a Socialist-led government.

"Today our big companies cannot live without alliances and especially European alliances...and modern countries cannot imagine their private companies teaming up with public companies subject to considerations that have nothing to do with the market," he said.

Chirac was responding to a question about Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's decision to halt the privatisation of defence electronics giant Thomson-CSF and keep a "decisive public shareholding" in the firm.

Jospin said last Friday that the privatisation initiated by his centre-right predecessors, who had planned to sell the firm to Lagardere or Alcatel Alsthom, would have served neither the national nor the staff's interests.

The government planned instead to build a French defence electronics pole around Thomson-CSF before looking for European allies and would put its policy into practice in the coming weeks, a statement from his office said.
Jospin has not yet announced what he plans to do about the last government's plans to sell a minority stake in France Telecom, suspended since he took office on June 3.
He has said he would consult the staff before any decision to sell stock in the state-owned telecommunications company.

Chirac did not mention Thomson or France Telecom by name but his comment about the need for alliances was a clear reference to those companies. To preserve French interests, such firms needed European alliances to compete with the giant American and Japanese conglomerates, he said.

A partial sale might allow firms such as Thomson-CSF and France Telecom to make key strategic alliances with European partners such as Britain's GEC and Germany's Daimler Benz Aerospace or Deutsche Telekom, which distrust France's traditional state direction of industry.
Lagardere hit back on Monday at weekend press reports that its rival, Alcatel Alsthom, would win a key role in Thomson-CSF.

The missiles-to-publishing empire headed by Jean-Luc Lagardere has now been thwarted in two bids for the company, which employs 46,000 people worldwide making radars, missile parts and communications.
It was the unlucky suitor in Chirac's botched first attempt to sell off the parent firm Thomson SA last year.
"Governments change but the same rumours are being repeated and still favour the same group, Alcatel," a Lagardere spokesman said, reading a prepared statement.
"Therefore, as happened last year, it is being said that they have won in advance before even the new process has begun."

French newspapers reported at the weekend that while keeping the state's current investment, the government was willing to see its percentage in Thomson-CSF fall indirectly below halfway to reach a blocking minority of around 40 percent.
That would allow extra capital to be found from private investors in an enlarged organisation or a new joint entity.
Newspapers said the new capital structure would be drawn from four main sources -- the government, state aerospace firm Aerospatiale, Alcatel Alsthom and Dassault.
Warplane manufacturer Dassault has teamed up with Alcatel in the Thomson discussions, providing what commentators said would be an attractive French solution for Jospin.

Chirac also criticised plans announced by Socialist Labour Minister Martine Aubry to restore the requirement for state labour inspectors to approve all layoff plans, abolished by a right-wing government in 1986.

"This debate is from another age...Today if we want to have a prosperous economy, employment and adapt to a changing world...we can no longer imprison the activities of those who create, invest and work in totally obsolete and absurd regulations," he said.
